We report the case of a 40-year-old woman who pre-
sented with a 9-year history of progressive left leg stiff-
ness. Initially she had difﬁculty walking at higher speeds,
and gradually developed marked rigidity in her right leg
and held it extended at the knee. Painful knee-extension
spasms were superimposed on submaximal extension
stiffness with emotional stimuli. Repeated magnetic reso-
nance imaging of the entire spinal cord and the brain
were normal. Routine laboratory tests were unremark-
able, apart from mildly elevated glucose levels. Immuno-
logical parameters were also negative. Four years after
the onset of symptoms she was tested for anti-GAD anti-
bodies and found to be positive, with a value of >500
U/ml (normal <7 U/ml).
Based on the clinical picture, the lack of symptom
spread over the years and the increased anti-GAD

antibody level, she was diagnosed with SLS. She was
started on diazepam 10 mg twice per day, but there was
only a modest effect on leg rigidity. She refused a dose
increase due to concerns about developing tolerance.
On neurological examination she had marked knee stiff-
ness (modiﬁed Ashworth scale score
4 ¼ 4) without other
abnormalities. On needle EMG recordings from the left
vastus medialis, continuous motor unit potential activity,
sometimes fusing into incomplete interference patterns,
was observed. Simultaneous recording from the antago-
nist hamstrings was not performed.
We administered a total of 400 U of botulinum toxin
A (BTX-A; Dysport; 50 U/0.05 ml) at 3 injection sites:
vastus lateralis 150 U; vastus medialis 150 U; and rectus
femoris 100 U. This rather low dose was chosen to pre-
vent knee joint instability. Clinical testing 3 weeks later
revealed no improvement. At a second session 4 months
later, we increased the dose to 550 U (vastus lateralis 200
U, vastus medialis 200 U, and rectus femoris 150 U),
which resulted in moderate improvement in rigidity that
was notable on physical examination. At the next session
(4 months after the second session) we further increased
the dose to 900 U (vastus lateralis 350 U, vastus medialis
350 U, and rectus femoris 200 U). This led to a dramatic
improvement in rigidity (Table 1) and gait, which was
associated with relief from painful extension spasms.
The clinical improvement reached a maximum 5
weeks post-injection. Apart from slight extension weakness
of the left leg that was evident only when she tried to
jump, the patient did not report any side effects. Marked
improvement lasted 2.5 months, and symptoms returned
to the pre-injection level 3 months later. Treatment was
then repeated with the same dose (900 U) injected in the
same muscles, resulting in a similar marked improvement.
Widely used symptomatic therapies for SPS include
diazepam and baclofen, whereas immunomodulatory treat-
ment consists mainly of intravenous immunoglobulin. Cor-
ticosteroids or plasmapheresis, and recently rituximab, can
be equally effective in some cases.
1,5 BTX-A is rarely used
in SPS, although positive clinical effects have been seen.6,7
Liguori et al.7 followed 2 patients for 2 years and reported
sustained BTX-A beneﬁt on repeated injections and a tend-
ency for increased improvement duration (up to 7
months) after each session.
Therapeutic data on SLS are scarce due to the rarity of
the syndrome. Treatments reported so far include diaz-
epam, clonazepam, baclofen, immunoglobulins, cortico-
steroids, plasmapheresis, cyclophosphamide, and gaba-
pentin, with varied efﬁcacy.
8–12 Injection of 900 U BTX-A
(Dysport) in the affected quadriceps muscle resulted in a
marked functional improvement with negligible side
effects in our patient, who had a 9-year history of typical
SLS. Due to its focal nature, SLS may be more suitable for
treatment with intramuscular botulinum toxin injections
than SPS. It should be noted, however, that anti–GAD-
antibody-positive SLS is an autoimmune disorder and
belongs to the clinical spectrum of SPS. BTX-A is not
expected to prevent progression into SPS, and therefore
tolerable immunological therapies (such as immunoglo-
bulins) should be tested for long-term treatment.
